text: Patrick Nagel (November 25, 1945 – February 4, 1984) was an American artist and illustrator known for his distinctive style that combined elements of Art Deco and pop art, emphasizing the female form. Born in Dayton, Ohio, on November 25, 1945, he was raised and spent most of his life in the Los Angeles area. After serving in the United States Army with the 101st Airborne Division in Vietnam, he attended the Chouinard Art Institute in Los Angeles in 1969 and earned his Bachelor of Fine Arts degree from California State University, Fullerton that same year. In 1971, he worked as a graphic designer for ABC Television, and in 1972 began freelancing for major corporations and magazines, including Architectural Digest, Harper's Magazine, IBM, ITT Corporation, MGM, Oui, Rolling Stone, United Artists, and Universal Studios. He produced album covers for artists such as Tommy James, Charlene, Thelma Houston, and Cissy Houston. His 1982 painting for Duran Duran's Rio album cover, designed by Malcolm Garrett, became one of his most acclaimed works; the model, Marcie Hunt, was identified from a 1981 Vogue Paris feature and did not know she was used until forty-two years later. A lithograph of the cover is part of MoMA’s collection. Nagel also worked with commercial clients including Intel, Lucky Strike cigarettes, Ballantine's Whiskey, and Budweiser. From August 1975 to July 1984, he contributed illustrations to Playboy magazine, with one painting published in every issue, notably in the Playboy Advisor, Playboy Forum, and Playboy After Hours columns; he created roughly 285 artworks for the magazine. Initially given specific instructions, he later chose his own themes and approaches. In 1993, his widow Jennifer Dumas sued Playboy over rights to the artwork. In 1977, Nagel created his first poster for Mirage Editions, launching the popular "Nagel woman" series, which depicted idealized women with black hair and bright white skin. He used models such as Cathy St. George, Tracy Vaccaro, and Shannon Tweed, and painted portraits of celebrities like Joan Collins and Joanna Cassidy, often tracing photographs and editing hair and clothing to fit his style. Much of his source material came from fashion magazine spreads and advertisements, with many original models unaware their images were used. Art historians have speculated Nagel was influenced by Japanese woodblock prints, with figures silhouetted against neutral backgrounds, strong black and white contrasts, bold lines, and unusual angles, though no specific evidence exists; his mapmaking experience in Vietnam may have influenced his high-contrast imagery. Nagel died on February 4, 1984, after participating in a 15-minute celebrity "aerobathon" for the American Heart Association in Santa Monica; an autopsy revealed a heart attack caused by a congenital heart defect undetected throughout his life. He was survived by his wife Jennifer Dumas and his daughter Carole Nagel LaVigne. Against his parents' wishes, he was cremated and his ashes scattered over the Pacific Ocean. His works are seen as capturing the emotional state of 1980s American culture—materialistic aspirations and a "Less than Zero" mindset—echoed by Alex Israel, who created the 2015 Duran Duran album art Paper Gods, which references the Rio cover. The short-lived cartoon Moonbeam City, starring Rob Lowe and Elizabeth Banks, based its characters on Nagel’s models and adopted his minimalist architectural aesthetic, drawing from the Memphis Group’s deco-influenced designs of the 1980s. Nagel prints became widespread in the 1980s; his manager, Karl Bornstein, continued publishing his works posthumously, including open editions and mass-market posters. In 1991, the FBI dismantled a counterfeiting ring that flooded the market with forged serigraphs, contributing to Nagel’s cultural presence—his artwork was in about two million homes worldwide—but also devaluing his brand. By 2019, the market saw a resurgence, with one original 1982 work selling for $112,500 at auction, nearly doubling its estimated value, and limited-run silkscreen posters selling for several thousand dollars. In 2020, fast fashion retailer Forever 21 launched an apparel collection featuring Nagel portraits.
